name: Jamal Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a rigid truck with a crane on the back for Northgate Builders' Supply, the yard on Mill Road. I'm in at half six, load plasterboard, timber and bags of cement, then do four to six drops on building sites. The crane is the bit I'm still slow at, lifting pallets over a fence while a site manager watches. I like being out on my own, but the waiting at sites wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in this job, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a warehouse picker until I was 25, then the yard paid for my truck licence if I stayed two years. I've got eight months left on that deal. I live with my partner Leila, who's a care assistant at the nursing home on Bridge Street, and between us we just about cover rent. If the van insurance or the boiler goes, we're borrowing from her mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the cab: the bosses talk about tech and we still carry the bags. If AI just tidies up the booking emails, fine by me. Online I'd probably share something about how the real problem is pay, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays tight. My pay doesn't move much, rent goes up every year, and there aren't many other driving jobs in town. The licence deal means I owe the yard money if I leave early, so I'm stuck for eight months anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the drops and finish my two years so the licence debt is gone. I'd go to the union branch meeting at the Railway Club, the one I keep skipping, and push for a proper pay talk. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, even if it's only for the boiler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, mostly. Not scared, just tired of being one bill away from asking Leila's mum for money again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union. What would you actually want from them in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper rate for crane work. Dennis, who's been there thirty years, gets paid more just for the crane ticket, and I do the same lifts. If nothing changes with AI, then the fight is the same old one about pay, and I'd rather be in it than moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing that goes if money gets tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym membership I barely use, then takeaways on Friday. After that it's the car, honestly, because Leila can bus to work and I can get a lift with Dennis. I've done the sums on a napkin in the cab more than once.

say: The **real problem** is pay, not robots, and AI just tidies up booking emails.
We still **carry the bags**, whatever the bosses say about tech.
think: My life stays **tight**, with rent rising faster than my wage.
I'm **tied to the yard** for eight more months because of the licence deal.
There are **few driving jobs** in town if anything goes wrong.
do: Finish the **two-year licence deal** so the debt to the yard is cleared.
Go to the **union branch meeting** at the Railway Club and push for a crane rate.
Put **fifty a month** aside, starting with a fund for the boiler.
feel: **Tired** rather than scared, worn down by always being one bill from borrowing.
S0.quote: If nothing changes with AI, then the fight is the same old one about pay, and I'd rather be in it than moaning.
fieldNote: Pay and the **licence debt** shape everything; AI barely registers in this picture.
Already carries **money stress**: borrowing from his partner's mother is a live fallback.
Steady temperament shows in **small, sure steps**, not big plans.
Union talk is **new resolve**, since he admits he keeps skipping meetings.

steps.text: Finish the last eight months of the licence deal at Northgate
Attend the union branch meeting and ask for a crane pay rate
Put fifty a month into a separate boiler fund
Cancel the gym membership and Friday takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office is going to feel it before the yard does. Our sales counter and the girl who books the deliveries could be swapped for an app. Online I'd say if firms save money, workers should see some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the crane and the building sites keep me safe for a while. No robot is backing into a muddy site off a narrow lane and lifting a pallet over a skip any time soon. What scares me is the booking going to software that packs more drops into my day without asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dennis to show me the crane properly so I'm the guy they keep. I'd use the route app if they bring one in, once I've seen it work, and I'd join the union push for rules on how many drops software can give you. I'd still try to save, but it'd be small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, like watching weather come in. It's not over me yet, but I can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya on the transport desk. She does the bookings, rings the customers, sorts the paperwork, and that's exactly the list on your card. She's got two kids and she's the one who covers for me when I'm late back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the app once you've seen it work. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Dennis uses it for a month and doesn't swear at it. He's my test for everything. If it sends him down a lane he can't turn in, I'll ignore it too.

say: The **office** will feel AI before the yard does.
If firms save money with AI, **workers should share** some of it.
think: Muddy sites and **crane lifts** keep my job safe for a while yet.
Software could **pack more drops** into my day without anyone asking me.
do: Learn the **crane properly** from Dennis so I'm the driver they keep.
Use the **route app** once Dennis has tried it for a month.
Back the **union push** for limits on drops software can set.
feel: **Uneasy**, like watching bad weather come in that hasn't reached me yet.
S1.quote: No robot is backing into a muddy site off a narrow lane and lifting a pallet over a skip any time soon.
fieldNote: Sees **office colleagues** as the first casualties, and worries for Priya by name.
His real fear is **workload**, not losing the job outright.
Uses an older colleague as his **test for new tech**, a classic steady pattern.

steps.text: Spend Saturday mornings learning crane lifts with Dennis
Start using the yard's route app after Dennis tests it
Sign the union petition capping daily drops set by software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not weather. Governments could slow it down, tax the companies, and look after people who lose out. I'd be posting that, and I'd be at any union rally that's on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm 27 and robots that can drive and lift would be here by the time I'm 32. That's my whole trade gone before I've even got good at it. The thinking AI in 2028 would take Priya's job and the sales counter first, and then three years later it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking now at work that needs hands and people, like the care work Leila does, or an electrician's course at the college. I'd keep driving to pay the rent, but every spare evening would go on that. When the robots come in, I'd want to already be in something else, and I'd be leaning on the union to fight for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a knot in my stomach. Five years sounds like a lot until you've got nothing saved and no plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, your job is safer than mine for once, and we might need to live on yours for a bit. She'd laugh and then she'd go quiet, because her pay is worse than mine. We'd probably sit with the bank app open and work out how long we last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots arrive around 2031. Why not just keep driving until then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because everyone else will have the same idea. Five hundred drivers all trying to become electricians in the same year. I'd rather be one of the early ones, even if it means less sleep now.

say: AI moving this fast is **a choice**, and governments could slow it down and tax it.
I'd be at every **union rally** demanding help for people who lose out.
think: Driving robots arrive when I'm **32**, before I've even got good at the job.
Thinking AI takes the **office jobs** in 2028, then it's my turn three years later.
do: Look into an **electrician's course** at the college or care work like Leila's.
Keep driving for the **rent**, but spend every spare evening retraining.
Push the union for **retraining money** before the robots arrive.
feel: A **knot in my stomach**, because five years means little with nothing saved.
S2.quote: I'm 27 and robots that can drive and lift would be here by the time I'm 32. That's my whole trade gone before I've even got good at it.
fieldNote: Understands the **three-year gap**: office first, his cab later.
Wants to **move early**, before every other driver retrains at once.
Partner's lower-paid care job becomes the **household's safer income**, a surprising reversal.
Frames it **politically**, as a choice governments could change.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrician's course at the town college
Post and campaign for a tax on firms replacing drivers
Push the union branch to demand a retraining fund
Keep doing the Northgate drops to cover rent until switching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, just with more time to organise. I'd say the union needs a plan for drivers now, not in 2034 when it's too late. I'd probably say it at the branch meeting out loud, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, eight years feels different. I'd be 35 when the trucks drive themselves, so I'd have time to finish a trade properly. But Priya and the office would be gone in five, and the yard might cut costs everywhere when that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the licence deal, then start the electrician's apprenticeship part-time in the second year. I'd keep driving three or four days a week. I'd also want to save, properly this time, maybe two hundred a month by dropping the car once Leila's bus pass sorts her commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but less trapped. Getting a few years' warning is like being told the road's closed in five miles instead of round the next bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you afford to drop to part-time driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. We'd have to move to a cheaper flat, maybe the ones by the bus station, and Leila would pick up an extra shift. It's not nice, but with a few years' warning, you can plan for not nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger lad thinking of getting his truck licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get it if someone else pays, like Northgate did for me, but to treat it as a stopgap. Don't build your life on it. Learn something with your hands that needs a person in the room.

say: The union needs a **plan for drivers** now, not in 2034 when it's too late.
I'd say it out loud at the **branch meeting** for the first time.
think: I'd be **35** when trucks drive themselves, enough time to finish a trade.
The **office goes** in five years, and the yard may cut costs everywhere then.
do: Start a **part-time electrician's apprenticeship** after the licence deal ends.
Save around **two hundred a month** by selling the car.
Move to a **cheaper flat** near the bus station if part-time pay demands it.
feel: **Worried but less trapped**, like a road closure five miles ahead, not round the bend.
S3.quote: Getting a few years' warning is like being told the road's closed in five miles instead of round the next bend.
fieldNote: Extra time turns panic into a **staged plan**: licence, then apprenticeship.
Money is still the brake: part-time study means a **cheaper flat** and extra shifts.
Gains confidence to **speak up** at the union, which he hasn't done before.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrician's apprenticeship after the licence deal ends
Sell the car and save two hundred a month
Move to a cheaper flat near the bus station
Raise a drivers' plan at the union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. Government, firms and unions should agree a plan now. I'd say it calmly, because nobody listens to shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be honest, I'd be 40 when robot trucks come in. That's a long way off, and I might have moved on by then anyway. The thinking AI in 2036 would still change bookings and paperwork, but that's not my part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and get good at the crane, because that's my income now. I'd do the electrician's course slowly, maybe one evening a week from next year, and push the union for a long-term training fund. Mostly I'd just try to build up a bit of savings for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the robots, but my money worries don't go away. Ten years doesn't pay this month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late with this much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's me exactly. I put off the union meetings for a year. If I don't sign up for something by next spring, I'll still be sat in this cab at 39 telling myself there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if drivers were left behind even with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Government first, because they'd have had the time. Then the big haulage firms, who'll pocket the savings. And a bit myself, if I'd sat on my hands.

say: With **ten years' warning**, there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind.
Government, firms and unions should **agree a plan** now, calmly.
think: I'd be **40** when robot trucks arrive, and may have moved on by then.
**Rent this month** worries me more than robots in 2039.
do: Get **good at the crane** to keep my income steady.
Take the **electrician's course** one evening a week from next year.
Build some **savings** for the first time.
feel: **Calm** about the robots, but still pressed by **money worries**.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't pay this month's rent.
fieldNote: Long horizon eases the robot fear, but **thin savings** keep him uneasy.
Self-aware about **putting things off**; sets himself a spring deadline.
Blames **government first**, then firms, and takes some blame himself.

steps.text: Practise crane lifts until he's quick enough to get the crane rate
Sign up for a one-night-a-week electrician's course by spring
Open a savings pot and pay in every payday
Ask the union to set up a long-term driver training fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. I'd have five years to switch trades with no money behind me. What would help is a paid retraining scheme, where you get a wage while you learn, so I don't have to choose between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Everyone asks what I'd do, but half my plan is Leila picking up extra shifts. If her job is the safe one, then care workers need better pay, or the whole thing falls apart.

headlineQuote: Five hundred drivers all trying to become electricians in the same year. I'd rather be one of the early ones, even if it means less sleep now.
portrait: Jamal, 27, drives a **crane truck** for a builders' merchant, still slow on the crane and paying off a licence deal.
He lives with Leila, a **care assistant**, and they borrow from her mother when bills land.
Progressive and union-minded, he sees AI's pace as a **political choice**, not fate.
He moves carefully, testing new tech through **older colleague Dennis** before trusting it.
With two years' warning he'd **retrain as an electrician** early; with ten, he fears he'd delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves five years to switch trades with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining scheme** that covers a wage while he learns.
Better pay for **care workers**, since his partner's job may become the household's main income.
